subject: Phrasing results for multi-species occupancy model

messages.author: 35f70018fb170472
messages.subject: Phrasing results for multi-species occupancy model
parts:
Hello all,

I have a question about phrasing when reporting results for a multi-species occupancy model. Apologies if this is pedantic, but I want to make sure I’m presenting things correctly.

I’ve modelled the data such that I have species-specific occupancy probabilities for each habitat type in my study area, and I’m then comparing the occupancy values between the habitat types. I’ve defined occupancy to be “the probability of a species using the area sampled by the camera trap during the survey period.”

I’ve been writing the results something like “Species-specific occupancy probability was higher for gibbons in Kerangas than in Low Pole.” But someone else wants to write is as “Gibbons were more likely to occupy Kerangas than Low Pole”, and I’m getting hung up on the “more likely to occupy”. I think I’m interpreting that phrase as “more likely to exist in Habitat X” which doesn’t feel quite right given the definition of occupancy probability. I also haven’t come across any papers that phrase the results in that way, so I’m unsure if it’s appropriate.

I may be overthinking this and am just confusing myself, but if anyone has thoughts on phrasing it that way, that would be appreciated!


Many thanks,
Shari

messages.author: bed9858844040a0b
messages.subject: Re: Phrasing results for multi-species occupancy model
parts: Hi Shari. I agree with your phrasing as well as your assessment of your co-author's alternative. Your co-authors phrasing makes it sound like you're talking about occupancy by the species of the whole region rather than a given sampling unit within that region. A compromise might be "Gibbons were more likely to occupy Kerangas sampling units than those in Low Pole."

Hi,
As far I know "occupancy probability" always refers to a 'site' rather than a 'species'. Thus,  I always type "site occupancy probability" or "species-specific site occupancy probability ". 

Best,
André

parts:
Dear Shari, Quresh,

I agree. Plus, that wording suggested by "someone" does actually not make any sense: if there is at least one gibbon in the Keranges as well as in the North Pole, then occupancy probability in both is equal to 1. Some reference to the sampling units, with which any measure of occupancy is inextricably linked, is really helpful.

Best regards  --- Marc

Shari
